11.1 · How Do We Measure Global Climate?

Review: Climate vs. Weather

  • Weather = short-term conditions (temperature, moisture, wind).
  • Climate = the long-term pattern of a region's weather (its averages, variability and extremes), usually measured over a standard 30-year period.
© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
11.1 · How Do We Measure Global Climate?

Weather vs. Climate Lab

11.1 · Proxies and Paleoclimates

Indirect Indicators of Ancient Climate

A proxy is an observable phenomenon that serves as an indirect indicator of past climate.

Tree Rings
Ring width records local growing conditions: a wide ring means a good year for that tree, whether warmth or water was the limit. Extend records hundreds to thousands of years.
Coral Skeletons
Growth rings and chemical signatures record past sea-surface temperatures and ocean acidity over centuries.
Ice Cores
Air bubbles preserve ancient atmosphere. ¹⁸O/¹⁶O isotope ratios reveal past temperatures, colder periods deplete heavier isotopes faster.
© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
11.2 · What Caused Climate Change in the Past?

What Caused Climate Change in the Past?

Fossil evidence of forested poles, 700-million-year-old tropical glaciers, and vast sea-level shifts reveal that Earth's climate has always changed, driven by forces very different from what we see today.

What Caused Climate Change in the Past?

Natural Drivers of Past Climate Change

Continental Drift

Continent positions alter solar radiation and ocean circulation. Mountain building draws CO₂ from the atmosphere via acidic rainfall.

Milankovitch Cycles

Orbital shape (100k yr), axial tilt and direction (26–40k yr) alter solar input, pacing ice ages and warm interglacial periods.

Biosphere Changes

Evolution of photosynthesizers, swamps, and forests has continuously altered atmospheric CO₂ and O₂ over geological time.

Eruptions & Asteroids

Krakatoa (1883) cooled Earth by a few tenths of a degree for several years. Siberian volcanism drove the Permian-Triassic mass extinction 252 million years ago.

11.2 · The Greenhouse Effect

Watch Earth Trap Heat

Change the carbon dioxide in the air, or remove every greenhouse gas, and watch the heat balance shift.

Carbon dioxide in the air
420ppm(today)
Model estimate: average surface temperature
+17°C
−20°C0°+25°C

Illustrative equilibrium model, not a measurement of today’s temperature. Surface temperature uses the standard climate-sensitivity relationship ΔT ≈ 3°C × log₂(CO₂ / 280 ppm), anchored to a pre-industrial average of about 15°C (estimates range from about 14 to 15°C). With no greenhouse gases Earth would be about −18°C, roughly 33°C colder than that average (as the textbook notes). Warming per doubling of CO₂: IPCC AR6 likely range 2.5–4°C.

11.4 · What's Happening with Our Climate Now?

Human-Driven Global Warming

The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (Working Group I, 2021) declared that "It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land."

54%
more greenhouse gas emissions in 2019 than in 1990 (IPCC AR6)
  • CO₂ concentrations are increasing: today's levels are far outside the natural range of the last 800,000 years.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over the last 800,000 years

Through eight ice ages and warm periods, CO₂ stayed between about 170 and 300 ppm. In 2025 it reached 426 ppm, about 43% above the highest natural level, and nearly all of that rise came in the last 150 years.

Distant past: air trapped in Antarctic ice cores (EPA compilation of various sources, 2022). Recent decades: direct air measurements, NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory (2026). Via Our World in Data. ppm = parts per million.
Carbon dioxide emitted by humans each year, 1750–2024

Yearly CO₂ from burning fossil fuels and making cement grew from 6 billion tonnes in 1950 to 38.6 billion in 2024. About 58% of all the CO₂ released this way since 1750 was emitted in 1990 or later.

Global Carbon Budget (2025), via Our World in Data. Annual CO₂ from fossil fuels and industry (including cement); land-use change, such as deforestation, is not included.

11.4 · Temperatures Are Increasing

Global Temperature Anomaly

How much warmer each year has been than the late-1800s average.

Global average temperature each year, 1850–2025, compared with 1861–1890

Every year since 1930 has been warmer than the 1861–1890 average, and the 10 warmest years on record have all come since 2015. 2025 came in at +1.41 °C. One year above 1.5 °C does not break the Paris limit, which is measured over about 20 years.

Met Office Hadley Centre, HadCRUT5 (2026), via Our World in Data. Annual global average near-surface temperature (land and sea), compared with the 1861–1890 average. Bar colours follow the warming-stripes scale, cool to warm.
11.4 · Other Greenhouse Gases Are Also Increasing

CO₂ and Beyond

Methane (CH₄)
About 27–30× the warming of CO₂, tonne for tonne, over 100 years; 166% above pre-industrial levels (2024). Sources: Coal mines, livestock, rice farming, landfills, gas leaks.
Nitrous Oxide (N₂O)
273× the warming of CO₂, tonne for tonne, over 100 years; lasts about 109 years; about 25% above pre-industrial levels (2024). Sources: Agricultural soils, fertilizer and manure, industrial processes, fossil fuel combustion.
Halocarbons (CFCs/HFCs)
Up to thousands of times more potent; no natural source; long lifetimes. Sources: Refrigerants, aerosols, solvents, fire retardants.

Concentrations: WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin No. 21 (2024 data). Warming per tonne (GWP100) and lifetimes: IPCC AR6 WGI, Chapter 7.

Each gas’s share of the extra heat trapped by human-caused increases in long-lived greenhouse gases since 1750 (2024).
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Annual Greenhouse Gas Index (2024): radiative forcing by gas.

11.5 · Effects — Precipitation and Extreme Weather

More Rain, More Drought, More Extremes

  • National Climate Assessment: heavy downpour frequency and intensity have increased over the past 3–5 decades in the US.
  • The Southwest and West face prolonged drought from higher evaporation, threatening agriculture and fueling wildfires.
  • Globally, intense heat waves are increasing mortality, especially in cities and among the elderly.

11.5 · Hurricanes and Severe Weather

Warmer oceans → more energy → more powerful storms

The National Climate Assessment predicts increasing hurricane intensity, especially in the Atlantic. Even as total storm counts may not always rise, the proportion of major (Category 3–5) hurricanes is growing. Thunderstorms, tornadoes, and winter storms are also affected.

  • Rising insurance premiums and property damage risk are reshaping housing markets now.
  • Heat waves intensify crop and livestock losses, especially in Texas and the Midwest.
  • Government disaster aid costs are growing as climate events become more frequent.
  • These costs (economic, social, and environmental) will only grow without action.
Top 10 costliest hurricanes in the United States, through 2020

9 of the 10 struck in 2004 or later. Part of the rise is exposure: more people and property now sit on the coast, and warmer oceans make the strongest storms stronger.

Estimated insured losses in billions of 2020 dollars, as ranked in 2020; later storms such as Ida (2021) and Ian (2022) are not included. Source: Insurance Information Institute, from Aon. Darker bars: 2004 or later.

11.5 · Effects — Ocean Acidification and Ecosystem Shifts

Ocean Acidification and Ecosystem Shifts

Polar bears, coral reefs, and migratory species among most visible indicators of ecological change.

Ocean Acidification
About 30% more acidic since industrialization (30% more hydrogen ions; pH has fallen about 0.1 and seawater is still alkaline), threatening coral and shellfish at the base of marine food webs.
Range Shifts
Species moving poleward and to higher elevations. Polar bears 'threatened' as sea ice habitat shrinks.
© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
11.5 · Effects: Ocean Acidification

Ocean Acidification: Seawater pH

Falling ocean surface pH as seawater absorbs more CO₂.

Surface seawater pH in the North Pacific, 1989–2024

Surface pH fell from 8.11 to 8.04 between 1989 and 2024. pH is logarithmic, so that drop means about 17% more hydrogen ions in the water. Seawater is still basic (above pH 7); it is becoming less basic as it absorbs CO₂.

Hawaii Ocean Time-series, Station ALOHA (about 100 km north of Oʻahu), School of Ocean & Earth Science & Technology, University of Hawaiʻi (2026), via Our World in Data. The vertical axis starts at pH 8.00 so the change is visible.
11.6 · What About the Future?

Climate Models, Scenarios & Tipping Points

  • Tipping Points: Thresholds where changes become self-reinforcing — permafrost methane release, ice sheet collapse — and may be irreversible. Early, deep action is therefore critical.
  • Climate models run simulations for different GHG emission scenarios, projecting outcomes to 2100.
  • Each scenario makes assumptions about future emissions, energy use, and population to project outcomes.
  • Positive feedbacks amplify change; understanding these dynamics is key to assessing risk.
  • Albedo: light surfaces (snow, ice) reflect heat; dark surfaces absorb it. Melting ice exposes dark ocean; a reinforcing feedback that amplifies warming.

11.7 · Climate Justice & Advocacy

Climate Inequities

Climate effects fall hardest on low-income communities, people of color, and Indigenous peoples, who contributed least to the problem.

  • Who emits: high-income countries are 15% of the world's people but produce 34% of its CO₂.
  • Who dies: deaths from floods, droughts and storms were 15 times higher in highly vulnerable regions (2010–2020).
  • Who loses income: warming has cut income per person by an estimated 17–31% in the countries home to the poorest 40% of people.
Share of global CO₂ emissions and of world population, by country income group

High-income countries hold 15% of the world’s people but emit 34% of its CO₂. Low-income countries hold 9% of people and emit less than 1%.

Global Carbon Budget and UN World Population Prospects, via Our World in Data (H. Ritchie, “There are huge inequalities in global CO₂ emissions,” May 2024). Fossil fuels and industry; land-use change not included. Countries are grouped by World Bank income group, not by the incomes of individuals within them.
Deaths from floods, droughts and storms, 2010–2020, compared with the least vulnerable regions

Death rates from these disasters were 15 times higher in highly vulnerable regions. About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in places highly vulnerable to climate change, with hotspots in West, Central and East Africa, South Asia, Central and South America, small island states and the Arctic.

IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group II (2022), Summary for Policymakers B.2 and B.2.4 (high confidence). Vulnerability is highest where poverty, weak public services, conflict and climate-dependent livelihoods overlap.
How warming since 1961 has changed income per person, compared with a world without it

Hotter, poorer countries have lost the most, while some cooler, wealthy countries may have gained. For most poor countries there is a greater than 90% chance that income per person is lower today than it would have been without global warming.

Diffenbaugh, N. S., & Burke, M. (2019). Global warming has increased global economic inequality. PNAS, 116(20), 9808–9813. “Poorest 40%” is the poorest four tenths of the world’s people, grouped by their country’s income per person. The bars in the gap chart are drawn to show the 25% difference.

So, Can We Afford It?

Two price tags per tonne: cutting greenhouse gases, and the damage carbon dioxide does.

The cost of acting
?
under $20
to cut one tonne of CO₂-equivalent
enough to halve 2019 emissions by 2030: all $100 or less
$0$100$200$300$400

The IPCC assessed enough cuts to halve global emissions from their 2019 level by 2030. More than half of that potential costs under $20 a tonne (solar, wind, efficiency, stopping methane leaks); all of it costs $100 a tonne or less, and some of it saves money.

IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Summary for Policymakers C.12.1 (net lifetime cost per tonne of CO₂-equivalent avoided)
The cost of not acting
?
$185
of damage from emitting one tonne of CO₂
$0$100$200$300$400

Lost lives from heat, lower crop yields, energy costs and sea-level rise, added up over the tonne’s lifetime (2020 dollars, 2% near-term discount rate). 5th–95th percentile range: $44 to $413. Even $44 is more than double the cost of over half of the cuts.

Rennert et al. (2022), “Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO₂,” Nature 610 (2020 dollars)

Chapter 11 · Key Concepts

Climate: How Does Global Climate Change?

Greenhouse Effect
GHGs trap outgoing heat, warming Earth's surface
Proxy / Paleoclimate
Indirect indicators of ancient climate (ice cores, tree rings)
Milankovitch Cycles
Orbital variations driving ice ages over tens of thousands of years
Thermohaline Conveyor
Global ocean circulation driven by temperature and salinity
ENSO (El Niño)
A coupled Pacific ocean–atmosphere cycle (El Niño and La Niña) that shifts weather worldwide
Albedo
Surface reflectivity — ice reflects; dark surfaces absorb heat
IPCC
UN body assessing climate science; 2021: human influence on warming is unequivocal
Phenology
Seasonal timing of biological activities — disrupted by warming
